tagline: The story of a prophet who ran from God's call, was swallowed and spared, preached to Israel's enemies, and was angry when God showed them mercy.
overview:
Jonah is unlike the other prophetic books. Most of them are collections of oracles with a little narrative; Jonah is almost entirely narrative, with only one short sentence of prophecy (3:4). It tells of Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet of Israel, whom God sends to preach against Nineveh, a great city of Assyria. Jonah runs the other way, boarding a ship for Tarshish at the far end of the known world. God hurls a storm at the sea, the pagan sailors throw Jonah overboard at his own request, and a great fish swallows him. From inside the fish he prays a psalm of thanksgiving, and the fish puts him out on dry land.

Given a second chance, Jonah goes to Nineveh and announces that in forty days it will be overturned. To everyone's surprise but God's, the whole city repents, from the king to the cattle, and God relents from the disaster he threatened. The last chapter is the real climax. Jonah is furious, and he explains why he ran in the first place: he knew God was gracious and compassionate and would forgive. God gives him a plant for shade, then takes it away, and ends the book with a question that Jonah never answers: should God not care about a great city full of people and animals?

Jonah matters because it turns the prophetic message back on the prophet and on the reader. The pagans in this book (sailors, a king, a whole city) respond to God more readily than God's own prophet does. The book asks whether we want God's mercy for ourselves only, and whether we can bear to see it given to people we fear or hate.
author: The book does not name its author. It tells the story about Jonah in the third person rather than in his own voice. Older Jewish and Christian tradition often assumed Jonah wrote it himself or that it came from prophetic circles close to him. Most modern scholars think it was written by an unnamed author some time after the events it describes, pointing to features of its Hebrew (some words and constructions more common in later Hebrew and Aramaic), to the description of Nineveh in the past tense ("Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city", 3:3), and to its reflective, carefully crafted form. Others answer that the linguistic evidence is inconclusive, since northern Israelite Hebrew may account for some unusual forms, and that the past tense can simply be narrative style.
date: The events are set in the eighth century BC. Jonah son of Amittai is mentioned in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet from Gath-hepher in Galilee who foretold the expansion of Israel's borders under King Jeroboam II (about 786 to 746 BC). The date of writing is debated. Those who read the book as written by Jonah or near his time place it in the eighth century. Many scholars date it after the exile, often in the fifth or fourth century BC, citing its language and its concern with how Israel should regard the nations, a live question in the Persian period. Others place it in between, in the seventh or sixth century. Whatever the date of writing, the book assumes that Nineveh was still standing and powerful, which it was until the Babylonians and Medes destroyed it in 612 BC.
setting:
In the eighth century BC Assyria, centered on the upper Tigris River in what is now northern Iraq, was the rising power of the ancient Near East. Its kings campaigned west toward Syria and the Mediterranean coast and were known for brutal treatment of conquered peoples. Nineveh was one of its great cities; it became the royal capital under Sennacherib around 700 BC. For Israel, Assyria was the enemy that would destroy the northern kingdom and its capital Samaria in 722 BC and later invade Judah. The prophet Nahum would celebrate Nineveh's fall.

The book's other places mark the edges of Jonah's world. Joppa (modern Jaffa, near Tel Aviv) was a port on Israel's coast. Tarshish lay far to the west; it is often identified with Tartessus in southern Spain, though some suggest Sardinia or another western site. To flee to Tarshish was to go as far from Nineveh, which lay to the east, as a ship could take you.
purpose: The book is aimed at readers who, like Jonah, know the right creed about God but resent its implications. Jonah can quote Israel's confession that God is "gracious and compassionate" (4:2, echoing Exodus 34:6), yet he is angry that this grace reaches Nineveh. The book shows God's concern for all people, including Israel's enemies, and it shows that God's warnings of judgment are meant to lead to repentance. Whether written in the eighth century for a prosperous Israel under Jeroboam II or in the Persian period for a community debating its relationship with the nations, it calls God's people to share God's own compassion. The open question at the end is addressed as much to the reader as to Jonah.
story: Jonah lived in the period covered by 2 Kings 14, when the northern kingdom of Israel enjoyed a last season of prosperity under Jeroboam II, the same years in which Amos and Hosea preached. Within a few decades Assyria would destroy that kingdom. In the canon Jonah stands fifth among the twelve Minor Prophets, between Obadiah (a judgment on Edom) and Micah. Its theme reaches back to God's promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and forward to the church's mission to the nations. Jonah's reluctance also anticipates the tension in Acts over whether Gentiles could be welcomed as they were.
christ:
Jesus himself used this book. When his opponents demanded a sign, he answered that "none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah" (Matthew 12:39). He explained: "For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). Jonah's descent and deliverance became a picture of Jesus' death, burial, and resurrection. Jesus also pointed to the Ninevites' repentance as a judgment on his own hearers, adding "now One greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41; compare Luke 11:29-32).

The contrasts are as important as the likeness. Jonah was thrown into the sea for his own disobedience, and his willingness to die saved the sailors almost despite himself; Jesus went into death in obedience and for others. Jonah resented God's mercy to the nations; Jesus wept over a city and sent his followers to all nations. The book's closing question about God's compassion is answered in the gospel, where God does not merely spare a city but gives his Son for the world.
reading:
Jonah is a carefully told story, full of irony, repetition, and surprise. Notice the word "great", which describes the city, the wind, the storm, the sailors' fear, the fish, Jonah's anger, and his joy. Notice how often Jonah goes "down" as he flees, and how God "appoints" a fish, a plant, a worm, and a wind. Notice that the pagans (sailors, king, city) are consistently more responsive to God than the prophet is. The book ends with a question, and the reader is meant to feel its weight.

The great debate about Jonah concerns its genre. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have taken it as historical narrative: Jonah is a real prophet known from 2 Kings 14:25, the story is told as events, and Jesus refers to Jonah and to the Ninevites as he refers to other historical figures, placing the men of Nineveh at the final judgment alongside the queen of the South. Many other scholars, including some who hold a high view of Scripture, read it as a didactic story or parable, pointing to its symmetry, its humor and exaggeration (fasting cattle in sackcloth), the lack of a named Assyrian king, and the absence of any Assyrian record of a mass repentance. They argue that Jesus could use a well-known story as an illustration without settling its genre. A third group holds both: a historical prophet and real events told with deliberate literary artistry and a teaching purpose. Whatever position a reader takes, the book's message is the same, and the worst misreading is to argue about the fish and miss the question about mercy with which the book ends.

structure.title: Jonah runs, and the sailors fear the LORD
structure.summary: Jonah flees toward Tarshish. God sends a storm, the sailors throw Jonah into the sea, the sea grows calm, and the sailors worship the LORD. A great fish swallows Jonah.

structure.title: Jonah's prayer from the depths
structure.summary: From inside the fish Jonah prays a psalm of thanksgiving for rescue from death. The fish puts him out on dry land.

structure.title: Nineveh repents
structure.summary: Jonah preaches a five-word warning in Hebrew. The whole city, led by its king, fasts and turns from violence, and God relents.

structure.title: Jonah's anger and God's question
structure.summary: Jonah is furious at God's mercy. God uses a plant, a worm, and a hot wind to teach him, and ends with a question about his compassion for Nineveh.

themes.title: God's compassion for the nations
themes.body: The book's final verse is its thesis: God cares about the great city of Nineveh, its people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and even its cattle. God's mercy is not the property of Israel. The sailors and the Ninevites, outsiders all, turn to him and are received.

themes.title: The reluctant prophet
themes.body: Jonah is not a hero. He runs, sleeps through the storm, preaches the shortest sermon in the prophets, and then sulks when it works. The book holds him up as a mirror to God's people, who can confess God's grace in words and resent it in practice.

themes.title: Judgment and repentance
themes.body: Jonah's message, "Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned", contains no offer of mercy, yet the Ninevites repent in hope, and God relents. The book shows that God's announcements of judgment are often conditional, meant to bring people to turn (as Jeremiah 18:7-8 explains). The Hebrew word for overturned can also mean turned around, and Nineveh is overturned, though not in the way Jonah expected.

themes.title: God's sovereignty over creation
themes.body: The LORD whom Jonah confesses as the God "who made the sea and the dry land" (1:9) commands wind, sea, fish, plant, worm, and east wind. Everything in the book obeys God except his prophet.

themes.title: Death and deliverance
themes.body: Jonah goes down to the depths, to the edge of Sheol, and God brings him up. His psalm in chapter 2 gives thanks for rescue from death, a pattern Jesus took up as a sign of his own death and resurrection.

keyChapters.why: Jonah's flight and the pagan sailors' turn to the LORD set up the book's central irony.
Jonah's prayer from the fish, the basis of Jesus' sign of Jonah, confesses that salvation is from the LORD.
Nineveh's repentance and God's relenting show that judgment announced is meant to lead to turning.
Jonah's anger at God's grace and God's closing question are the heart of the book.
